passage: The community hall smelled of rice and marigolds. It was the prayer meeting for Arohi's Nani. Aunties were cutting vegetables in the back, some wiping their eyes. Uncles sat on durries, singing slow bhajans. Arohi didn't understand all the words. She sat on her cousin Gargi's lap and watched. An old aunty she didn't know gave her a laddoo and stroked her head. Mummy was crying, but everyone kept coming to hug her. Gargi whispered, "Everyone came because they loved Nani." Arohi leaned back into Gargi. She felt wrapped up, like in a big warm blanket.

qa.q: What were the uncles doing?
qa.a: They sat on durries, singing slow bhajans.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel sitting on Gargi's lap?
qa.a: She felt sad but held and safe, wrapped up by all the family around her, even though she didn't understand everything.

qa.q: How might an adult help Arohi understand the gathering?
qa.a: They could explain simply, like Gargi did, that people came because they loved Nani and want to be together while they are sad.

qa.q: What is it like for Arohi's mother to be hugged by so many people?
qa.a: She is grieving, but the hugs likely help her feel supported and less alone. 🤍

grounding: At a prayer gathering after her grandmother dies, a young girl feels held by the community of relatives who cook, sing and cry together.

passage:
Day one: After Dadu died, the house filled with people. Rukmini hid behind the door. Everyone was crying, and she didn't know why they were all here.
Day four: Pema Aunty from next door brought a huge pot of dal. The aunties cooked together in the courtyard, talking softly. Someone let Rukmini stir the pot. She felt a little better.
Day thirteen: At the last prayers, everyone ate together on long mats. Mamma cried, then laughed at a story about Dadu. Rukmini sat between two cousins. "We're all Dadu's family," she said to herself.

qa.q: What did Pema Aunty bring on day four?
qa.a: She brought a huge pot of dal.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel on day one?
qa.a: She felt confused and scared, hiding behind the door because everyone was crying and she didn't know why.

qa.q: What helped Rukmini feel part of the gathering?
qa.a: Being given a small job stirring the pot, and sitting among cousins at the last prayers, let her join in.

qa.q: How might Mamma feel on day thirteen?
qa.a: She is still sad, but sharing stories and food with family lets her laugh as well as cry.

grounding: Over the mourning days after a grandparent's death, a young girl moves from confusion to feeling held by relatives who cook, pray and remember together.

passage: On the building terrace, Kiran found Dada's old walking stick behind the water tank. He sat down with it. "Mumma, Dada used to give me two jalebis every Sunday. And he told the story of the clever monkey." His voice wobbled, but he smiled a little too. His mother, Gurleen, sat beside him. "You feel happy and sad at the same time, hmm?" Kiran nodded. "Shall we make a book about Dada? You draw, I'll write." That evening Kiran drew Dada with jalebis and a monkey on his shoulder. "Now I won't forget," he said.

qa.q: What did Kiran find behind the water tank?
qa.a: He found Dada's old walking stick.

qa.q: How was Kiran feeling while talking about Dada?
qa.a: He felt warm and sad together; his voice wobbled, but he smiled a little too.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that a wise adult does after a loss?
qa.a: She named his mixed feelings and helped him make a drawing book so he could keep remembering Dada.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel reading Kiran's book later?
qa.a: She may feel moved and comforted, seeing that her son's love for Dada stays.

grounding: A young boy remembers his late grandfather's sweets and stories with mixed warmth and sadness, and his mother helps him draw a memory book.

passage:
"Didi, remember Dada's pocket? He always had toffees in it."
"I remember, Sachin. Orange ones."
"And he told me the elephant story." Sachin's eyes filled. "I'm sad. But I'm happy when I think of him."
Mumma came in with the washing. "Both feelings can live together."

qa.q: How did Sachin feel remembering Dada?
qa.a: He felt sad and happy together, warm when he thought of Dada and teary that he was gone.

qa.q: What did Aadhya and Mumma do that helped Sachin?
qa.a: They let him tell Dada's elephant story, listened, and planned to write it down to keep the memory.

grounding: A young boy remembers his late grandfather with warmth and sadness, and his family helps him tell and keep Dada's stories.

passage:
"Mummy?"
"Uday? It's late. Can't sleep?"
"Will you die too, like Nanu?"
Mummy sat on the bed and switched on the small lamp.
"That's a big question. Nanu was very old and very sick. Nearly everybody gets to grow very, very old. I'm healthy, and I plan to be here till you're big and even bigger."
"But what if?"
"If anything ever happened, Papa and lots of people would look after you. Always."
Papa, Deepak, leaned in the doorway. "Always."
Uday pulled Mummy's hand under his cheek. "Stay till I sleep?"
"I'll stay."

qa.q: What did Mummy switch on?
qa.a: She switched on the small lamp.

qa.q: Why did Uday ask if Mummy would die too?
qa.a: He felt frightened at night after Nanu's death and worried that he might lose Mummy too.

qa.q: What made Mummy's answer helpful?
qa.a: She answered honestly and calmly: most people live a long time, and Uday would always be looked after.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel hearing Uday's question from the doorway?
qa.a: He may feel tender and protective, wanting to add his own "Always" to reassure his son.

grounding: After his grandfather's death, a young boy asks his mother at night if she will die too, and she answers honestly and calmly.

passage:
Note from Rajni, Vijay's mummy, for his teacher.
Since Dadi died last month, Vijay wakes at night and cries. Two nights ago he asked, "Will you die too, Mummy?" At first I said "Don't talk like that," and he cried harder. Last night I tried again. I said, "Nearly everyone grows very, very old before they die. And you will always be looked after." He asked, "By who?" I named Papa, Bua and his Nana. He counted them on his fingers and went to sleep. If he asks you about death, please answer simply and calmly too.

qa.q: Whom did Rajni name as people who would look after Vijay?
qa.a: She named Papa, Bua and his Nana.

qa.q: How was Vijay feeling when he woke at night crying?
qa.a: He felt frightened and worried since Dadi died, afraid that his mother might die too.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what worked better?
qa.a: Saying "Don't talk like that" made him cry harder; an honest, calm answer that most people live long and he'd be looked after helped him settle.

qa.q: How might Vijay's teacher use this note?
qa.a: The teacher can be ready to answer his questions about death simply and calmly, as his mummy asked.

grounding: After his grandmother dies, a young boy asks his mother if she will die too; hiding the question upsets him, and an honest, calm answer helps.

passage:
"Ammi, look! My sharara is shiny!"
"Eid Mubarak, Rehana! Turn round."
Rehana spun until she was dizzy. Outside, the whole lane smelled of sewaiyan. Uncles were hugging three times.
"Eid Mubarak, Rehana!" called Hemant from next door, holding his mother's hand.
"Hemant, come! Ammi made sewaiyan!"
Rehana held her little bowl and watched the lane. Everyone had new clothes. Everyone was smiling.
"Ammi, is everybody having Eid?"
"Everybody in our family, and in our mosque, and friends like Hemant too."
Rehana grinned. "It's a big Eid."

qa.q: What did the lane smell of?
qa.a: It smelled of sewaiyan.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel spinning in her new sharara?
qa.a: She felt joyful and excited, part of something big as everyone around her celebrated.

qa.q: How could Ammi help Rehana feel even more part of Eid?
qa.a: She could tell her simple stories of what Eid means to their family, as she began to do.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemant to be invited for sewaiyan?
qa.a: Hemant probably feels welcome and happy to share his neighbour's festival.

grounding: On Eid, a young girl in new clothes feels joyful and part of something big with family, community and friends.

passage:
From Gargi Chithi's festival diary.
Diwali at Paati's house. Minakshi wore her new green pavadai and wouldn't stop twirling. At dawn, when the elders gave the oil bath and the first cracker burst, she hid behind me, then laughed. I let her light the first lamp with my hand over hers. All evening she ran from lamp to lamp, counting them. At dinner she told everyone, "This is our family Diwali! Paati's lamps and Chithi's lamps and my lamps!" Paati told her the story of the lamps. She fell asleep in her new clothes.

qa.q: What colour was Minakshi's new pavadai?
qa.a: Her new pavadai was green.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel at dinner when she spoke about "our family Diwali"?
qa.a: She felt happy and proud, part of something big that belonged to her whole family.

qa.q: What did Gargi do to help Minakshi join the celebration?
qa.a: Gargi let her light the first lamp with a guiding hand, giving her a real part in the festival.

qa.q: How might Paati feel telling Minakshi the story of the lamps?
qa.a: Paati likely feels warm and proud to pass the family's festival story on to her granddaughter.

grounding: At Diwali, a young girl in new clothes feels she belongs to her family and its traditions through lamps, food and stories.

passage: At the wedding in the big Kolkata hall, the grown-ups danced and the cousins ran wild. Aadhya and four cousins played hide and seek under the tables until midnight. They giggled so hard that Aadhya's tummy hurt and she had to lie on the carpet. Then Nirmala Mausi noticed little Tuktuk sitting alone by the stage, holding her balloon. Mausi scooped her up and brought her over. "Tuktuk can hide with you. She's very good at being quiet." Aadhya grabbed Tuktuk's hand. "You're on my team!" Tuktuk hid so well nobody found her, and she laughed loudest of all.

qa.q: Where did the cousins play hide and seek?
qa.a: They played hide and seek under the tables until midnight.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel playing with her cousins?
qa.a: She felt pure joy; she giggled so hard her tummy hurt.

qa.q: What did Nirmala Mausi do that made the fun better?
qa.a: She noticed quiet Tuktuk alone and brought her into the game, giving her a strength to be proud of. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tuktuk feel when Aadhya says "You're on my team"?
qa.a: Tuktuk likely feels included and happy after sitting alone, and laughs loudest of all.

grounding: A young girl laughs with her cousins all night at a wedding, and an aunt makes sure a quieter cousin is included.

passage:
"Kamal, it's your turn to be the ghost!"
"Wooooo!" Kamal flapped a bedsheet over his head, and all the cousins shrieked and ran across the courtyard.
"Again! Again!"
Kamal laughed so much his tummy hurt. Then he saw Bidisha by the pillar, not running.
"Bidisha, why aren't you playing?"
"It's too loud."
Their Pishi was stringing lights nearby. "Bidisha, would you like to be the ghost's helper? You can hold the torch."
Bidisha thought, then took it. When she shone it on Kamal, everyone screamed with laughter, and Bidisha giggled too.

qa.q: What did Kamal flap over his head?
qa.a: He flapped a bedsheet over his head.

qa.q: How was Kamal feeling as the cousins shrieked and ran?
qa.a: He felt pure joy and fun, laughing so much his tummy hurt.

qa.q: How did Pishi include Bidisha in a way that suited her?
qa.a: She offered a quieter job, holding the torch as the ghost's helper, so Bidisha could join without being in the loud chase.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see the ghost game at first?
qa.a: She finds it too loud, so she stays by the pillar until she is given a gentler role.

grounding: A young boy plays and laughs with his cousins during a festival, and an aunt helps a quieter cousin join in.

passage: On the night of Diwali, cousin Akash came from the town with a whole box of sparklers and flowerpots. Irawati had six small sparklers. Akash's flowerpot shot up into a fountain of gold. Everyone cheered. Irawati felt a sting in her chest. She sat on the doorstep, lip out, and would not light hers. Her Amma sat beside her. "You wish you had a big box too?" Irawati nodded hard. "It's okay to wish. We have what we have. And I love you with or without fountains." Amma held out a sparkler. Irawati lit it and drew a slow circle in the dark.

qa.q: How many sparklers did Irawati have?
qa.a: Irawati had six small sparklers.

qa.q: What did Irawati feel when Akash's flowerpot shot up?
qa.a: She felt a sting of envy in her chest and sulked on the doorstep.

qa.q: Why was Amma's reply wise?
qa.a: She accepted Irawati's wish instead of scolding, was honest that they have what they have, and reminded her she is loved.

qa.q: How might Akash see Irawati sulking?
qa.a: He may not even notice, busy with his fireworks, or he may feel a little awkward that she looks sad.

grounding: A young girl feels envy at her cousin's bigger fireworks and sulks, and her mother accepts the wish and reminds her she is loved.

passage: On Christmas morning in Johannesburg, Abebe's cousin Lindiwe arrived in a shiny purple dress with a sparkly bow. Abebe looked down at his shirt. It was new, but plain blue. Lindiwe spun, and all the aunties clapped. Abebe felt a sting. He went and sat under the table with his arms folded. Mama crouched and peeped in. "You wish your clothes were shinier?" "Hers is better." "It's okay to wish. We have what we have. And I love you in any shirt." Abebe peeked at Mama's smile, then crawled out. "Can I have the first slice of cake?"

grounding: A young boy feels envy at his cousin's fancier festival clothes, and his mother accepts the feeling and reassures him of her love.

passage: In the flat across the hall in Leicester, Sami's family was celebrating Eid. Lindiwe stood at their open door, holding her mum's hand. The flat was full of people and a smell of cardamom. passage: The building's community hall was full of drums and flowers. Eshaan's family had brought their Ganpati there for all the neighbours. Dilnaz peeped in with her mummy. passage:
"Mumma, how long is the puja?"
"A little long today, Sarika."
Sarika wriggled on the mat. The priest's words went on and on. She yawned. She poked Trisha, her cousin.
"Sit still," Trisha whispered.
"I'm bored," Sarika whispered back.
Mumma leaned over. "Want a job? When Panditji rings his bell, you ring yours."
"Why?"
"The bell says, 'We're here, we're listening.'"
Sarika held the small bell tight. Every time the big bell rang, she rang hers, very seriously. At the end, Mumma said, "Now touch Nani's feet. It means 'bless me'."

qa.q: What job did Mumma give Sarika?
qa.a: When Panditji rang his bell, Sarika should ring hers.

qa.q: How was Sarika feeling before she got the bell?
qa.a: She felt bored and restless, wriggling, yawning and poking her cousin.

qa.q: What did Mumma do that made the ritual easier to join?
qa.a: She gave Sarika a small role and explained simply what the bell and touching feet mean.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Sarika's wriggling?
qa.a: Trisha may feel a bit embarrassed and want Sarika to sit still, since she whispers to her to stop.

grounding: A young girl is bored during a long puja, and her mother gives her a small role and explains simply why.

passage:
Note from Himani, Joseph's mother, in our family notebook.
At Nana's housewarming puja today, Joseph sat on the mat for about five minutes, then started rolling, humming and pulling at the flower garland. When I asked him to touch Nana's feet, he hid behind me. "Why?" I explained, "It's like saying, 'Please bless me.'" Then I gave him the plate of flower petals to hold for the priest. He sat up straight and handed petals one by one. At the end he touched Nana's feet on his own. Nana laughed and blessed him twice.

qa.q: What did Himani give Joseph to hold?
qa.a: She gave him the plate of flower petals to hold for the priest.

qa.q: What does Joseph rolling and humming suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt bored and restless during the long puja and didn't understand what was happening.

qa.q: What helped Joseph join the ritual with understanding?
qa.a: Himani explained simply what touching feet means and gave him a small, real job with the petals.

qa.q: How might Nana feel when Joseph touches his feet on his own?
qa.a: Nana likely feels delighted and touched, which is why he laughs and blesses him twice.

grounding: A young boy is restless in a long puja and unsure about touching elders' feet, until his mother explains simply and gives him a role.

passage: At the temple's Sunday class, Preeti wouldn't pick up her crayons. "I broke a cup at home," she whispered to Keerthana Aunty, the teacher. "My cousin said God saw and God is angry. qa.a: She broke a cup at home.

qa.q: How was Preeti feeling when she wouldn't pick up her crayons?
qa.a: She felt worried and frightened that God was angry and would punish her.

qa.q: What did Keerthana Aunty do to ease Preeti's fear?
qa.a: She stressed kindness and forgiveness, linked it to Mummy forgiving her and told a forgiving story.

qa.q: Why might Preeti's cousin have said God is angry?

grounding: A young girl fears God will be angry about a broken cup, and a teacher stresses kindness and forgiveness to ease her worry.

passage:
From the lunch notes of the Tiny Tots daycare, by the lunch teacher.
Today, before eating, Parveen folded her hands and said quietly, "Thank you for my food." Kalyani, sitting next to her, asked, "Who are you saying thank you to?" Parveen said, "To Allah and to Ammi who made it." Kalyani folded her hands too. "Thank you to the farmer," Kalyani said. Soon the whole table was saying thank you, to God, to mums, to cooks, to the sun. Parveen looked calm and happy as she opened her tiffin. We may make this a daily moment.

qa.q: Whom did Kalyani thank?
qa.a: Kalyani thanked the farmer.

qa.q: How did Parveen seem when she opened her tiffin?
qa.a: She looked calm and happy after her quiet thank-you prayer, feeling grateful.

qa.q: Why might a daily thank-you moment suit a mixed class?
qa.a: Each child can thank in their own way, to God, family, farmers or the sun, so everyone feels included whatever their family believes.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Parveen's prayer?
qa.a: Kalyani seems curious and inspired by it, joining in with her own kind of thanks. 😊

grounding: A young girl says a simple thank-you prayer before eating, feels calm and grateful, and classmates join in their own ways.

passage: In the farmhouse kitchen, the rotis were stacked high and the dal was steaming. Anand's Amma, Rekha, sat down on the mat. Before anyone ate, the family folded their hands. "Thank you to the cow for the ghee." Everyone smiled. Anand opened his eyes and felt still and warm inside, like the rotis. Then he tore off a piece and dipped it in the dal.

qa.a: Dadi said thank you to the rain.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after saying his thank-you?
qa.a: He felt calm and grateful, still and warm inside, like the rotis.

qa.q: What does this family's habit teach Anand?
qa.a: It teaches him to notice and thank the people and things that bring his food, even without praying to anyone special.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel when Anand thanks the cow?
qa.a: She probably feels amused and proud that he has made the gratitude his own.

grounding: A young boy says thank you before eating with his family, who give thanks without a particular faith, and feels calm and grateful.
